column3: It exactly repeats that this attained good is granted only to the patient, directly clarifying the focus verse's closing condition.
It joins patience and righteous deeds with forgiveness and a great reward, closely reinforcing the focus verse's promised return.
It states that the patient receive their reward without measure, expanding the scale of the focus verse's divine reward.
Its command for beautiful patience supports the focus verse's required patience but adds no reward or wealth contrast.
Those given knowledge and faith recognize the resurrection, supplying an eschatological horizon for the knowledgeable speakers' valuation.
It binds patience to sincere worship and resisting worldly adornment, directly countering the display that prompted the focus verse.
It denies that wealth and children bring nearness and makes faith and righteous deeds the basis for multiplied reward.
It presents divine reward in this world and the next for good-doers, a close but less specific reward parallel.
It pairs faith and righteous action with the fairest reward, reinforcing the focus verse's qualifying formula.
The command to purify clothing does not illuminate knowledge, reward, patience, or Qarun's wealth.
Knowledge held in the learned provides a limited role parallel without the focus verse's moral valuation.
Its just economic conduct is called better for believers, offering an ethical alternative to valuing gain by worldly display.
Repentance, faith, and righteous deeds lead to Paradise, supporting the focus verse's conditions for a better outcome.
It redirects desire from worldly attractions to a better enduring divine reward for the God-conscious.
It associates faith and righteous deeds with reward from God and freedom from fear, broadly supporting the focus formula.
Patience appears among devotional virtues but without its relation to reward or visible wealth.
Its faith-and-righteous-deeds formula is a broad parallel already supplied more directly by earlier cards.
It explicitly says God's reward is better for those who believe and are mindful, very closely echoing the focus revaluation.
The learned recognize truth and then believe, supporting the focus verse's association of knowledge with faithful judgment.
Its contrast of evil recompense is only a distant inverse of the focus verse's better divine reward.
It directly contrasts seeking worldly reward with God's possession of both worldly and final reward.
Its ruler treats God-given means as better than payment, but it does not address the focus verse's reward or patience.
It combines faith, righteous deeds, mutual truth, and mutual patience as the alternative to loss.
A people misuse ease and are scattered, while patient gratitude is preserved, giving a social contrast to attraction by prosperity.
It distinguishes the reward sought in this world from that of the hereafter and promises recompense to the grateful.
God rewards faithful recognition with enduring gardens, a concrete instance of reward for good action.
Knowledge followed by rivalry marks a boundary case: knowledge alone does not secure the faithful judgment voiced in the focus verse.
Patience is called better, but the social etiquette setting adds little to the focus verse's reward horizon.
Demanding a treasure or garden as proof exposes the same attraction to visible wealth that the focus verse corrects.
It explicitly sets worldly wealth and children below lasting righteous deeds in reward and hope.
After worldly loss, it declares God best in reward and outcome, a close but already covered divine-reward contrast.
Covering ears and garments during Noah's call does not add to the focus themes.
Musa's warning, "woe to you," and threat of punishment frame a related corrective rebuke against false claims.
Patience and piety resist hostile scheming, but the conflict setting is remote from reward over wealth.
It calls worldly enjoyment little and the hereafter better for the God-conscious, reinforcing the focus's comparative horizon.
Patience and reliance in migration offer a secondary example without a reward or value comparison.
The dispute over prayer direction and following desires does not clarify the focus verse.
Patience and piety condition military support, a distinct application of patience.
Its communal command to good gives only a broad background to calling something better.
Patience for the Lord directly supports the focus verse's final requirement, though without its reward frame.
God expands and restricts provision and replaces charitable spending, correcting self-grounded readings of wealth.
Isma'il's willingness to be patient is a distinct trial narrative with limited explanatory value here.
Affluent leaders deny the meeting of the hereafter, a sharp narrative contrast to the knowledgeable revaluation in the focus verse.
Patience in the Fire cannot alter the outcome, serving only as a contrast to patience that receives reward.
Patient forgiveness is called resolute conduct, adding an ethical form of the patience named in the focus verse.
Calling revealed adjudication better is only a broad analogue to calling God's reward better.
The deniers' arrogance and demands for signs have no direct reward, righteous-deeds, or patience connection.
It declares God better and more enduring than Pharaoh's threat, directly sharpening the focus verse's comparative claim.
The warning scene of final punishment supplies the accountability horizon behind preferring God's reward.
Seeking help through patience and prayer offers a practical support for sustaining the patience the focus verse requires.
Patience is called better in a marriage-law concession, a remote application of the term.
Musa's pledge to patience introduces patience as disciplined restraint in the presence of knowledge not yet understood.
It calls the hereafter's abode better for those who do good, supporting the focus verse's longer-term valuation.
The prayer for patience and steadfastness presents patience as strength supplied by God under pressure.
The oppressed believers' response to arrogant elites gives a limited social parallel to Qarun's audience.
It shows that patience is difficult where reasons are not yet disclosed, qualifying the focus verse's demanding condition.
Calling to God, righteous action, and Muslim commitment form a close ethical counterpart to the focus's faith-and-deeds condition.
Loss of wealth and goods tests people, while glad tidings are for the patient, directly contextualizing patience amid material change.
Forgiveness follows repentance, faith, righteous deeds, and guidance, broadly reinforcing the focus verse's qualifying path.
It calls lasting righteous deeds better in reward and return, closely matching the focus verse's measure of value.
Believers who do righteous deeds receive good news and an increase for each good act, a related reward dynamic.
It defines true righteousness through faith, costly giving, and endurance, giving substance to the focus verse's righteous action.
Qarun claims his wealth came through his own knowledge and ignores earlier destruction, directly setting up the focus verse's corrective reply.
The list of exemplary figures as good adds no specific connection to reward, patience, or Qarun.
Its same-surah formula of repentance, faith, and righteous action leading to success reinforces the focus verse's conditions.
A better replacement after apparent loss supports the possibility that divine goodness exceeds the visible present.
Its claim that knowledge belongs to God gives only a general boundary for the focus verse's learned speakers.
It directs believers to seek help through patience and prayer and affirms God's presence with the patient.
A witness possessing knowledge of the Book offers a limited learned-person parallel without the focus's valuation.
The prayer for forgiveness and mercy does not add to the focus verse's reward, work, or patience relation.
God fully pays the wages of believers who do righteous deeds, a direct but general reward parallel.
The chosen righteous figures provide only a general positive valuation.
God's comprehensive knowledge does not specifically illuminate the learned believers' statement or divine reward.
Faith and striving with wealth and selves are called better, redirecting valued possessions toward a divinely judged gain.
It contrasts believers who do righteous deeds with evildoers, supporting the focus verse's moral distinction.
The river test shows disciplined restraint amid available abundance and closes by affirming God with the patient.
Knowledge, faith, and testing occur together, but the fire-keeper number does not clarify the focus verse.
It commands patience until God's judgment between divided believers and deniers, adding a judicial form of patience.
Repentance joined to righteous action is relevant but redundant after several fuller faith-and-deeds reward passages.
The Prophet's merciful listening does not bear on the focus verse's reward or patience.
God raises believers and those given knowledge in ranks, supporting the dignified role of knowledge in the focus verse.
Every atom's good deed is seen, grounding the focus verse's promise that righteous action has a return.
The learned announce disgrace for disbelievers on the Last Day, only broadly sharing the learned-speaker setting.
Paradise is given in recompense for patience, directly confirming patience's rewarded outcome.
Repentance, faith, and righteous action transform evil deeds to good, a related account of divine recompense.
Those tested, striving, and patient receive forgiveness and mercy, an applied endurance-and-reward pattern.
Those given knowledge recognize revelation as truth and guidance, a close knowledge-to-right-judgment parallel.
A good final abode is explicitly linked to what believers patiently endured.
Those given prior knowledge respond to recitation with worship, showing knowledge expressed in faithful recognition.
The threatened destruction of an admired garden and hope for a better gift from God parallels correction of wealth-based confidence.
The adorned worldly life deceives disbelievers, while the God-conscious are above them in the final judgment.
It commands patience for God's judgment under divine care, supporting patient trust in an outcome not yet visible.
The warning against hearing without listening has no material connection to the focus verse.
Patience enables a small force in battle, a distant and specialized application of patience.
Inheritance shares in family law do not clarify divine reward or the Qarun episode.
The Messenger's lack of financial demand and God as best provider are too remote from the focus verse.
The rebuke for laughing rather than weeping does not add to the focus themes.
Beautiful patience before deception gives a general endurance parallel but lacks the reward-and-wealth contrast.
Its ban on defrauding people and spreading corruption supplies an economic ethical contrast to wrongful valuation of wealth.
Patience toward hostile speech is a distant application of the focus verse's patience requirement.
Qarun's transgression, immense treasures, and the warning not to exult establish the narrative problem answered by the learned in 28:80.
It directly commands using God-given wealth to seek the final abode, doing good, and avoiding corruption, supplying the focus verse's ethical program.
Those desiring worldly life envy Qarun's great fortune, immediately setting up the corrective valuation spoken in 28:80.
God causes Qarun and his dwelling to be swallowed, demonstrating that displayed wealth cannot secure its possessor.
The former admirers learn that God expands and restricts provision and that success does not belong to deniers, completing 28:80's correction.
The final abode belongs to those who seek neither exaltation nor corruption on earth, giving the end-state of the focus verse's value judgment.
Whoever brings good receives better than it, directly supporting the focus verse's claim that divine reward is better.
It forbids extending one's gaze toward worldly splendor and declares the Lord's provision better and more enduring.
What is given in this world is temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting.
The one promised a good promise and meeting it is contrasted with one merely enjoying worldly life before being brought for judgment.
It rebukes contentment with worldly life in place of the hereafter and calls worldly enjoyment little by comparison.
Those who seek worldly life and its adornment receive their deeds here, framing the limitation of a worldly reward horizon.
It states that those devoted only to worldly life have no share in the hereafter and their works come to nothing.
Worldly life is only enjoyment when set beside the hereafter, reinforcing the focus verse's longer horizon.
It identifies those who prefer worldly life to the hereafter and turn others from God's way, a direct negative counterpart.
What people possess perishes while what is with God remains, and the patient receive recompense according to their best deeds.
A believer who does righteous work receives a good life and a reward according to the best of what was done.
Seeking the immediate world brings only a limited allotted result before punishment, exposing the inadequacy of short-term valuation.
Seeking the hereafter, striving for it, and believing leads to a grateful reception, closely complementing the focus verse's conditions.
Worldly life is diversion and play, while the final abode is the true life, broadly reinforcing the focus perspective.
It warns that worldly life must not deceive, directly addressing the pressure of visible display behind the focus verse.
Worldly life is temporary enjoyment, whereas the hereafter is the enduring abode.
Those who seek the harvest of the hereafter receive increase, while those seeking the worldly harvest have no share in the hereafter.
Earthly houses, roofs, stairs, and ornaments are presented as worldly enjoyment, while the hereafter with God belongs to the mindful.
Worldly life is play, adornment, boasting, and competition in wealth, while forgiveness and great reward provide the decisive alternative.
It calls believers to race toward forgiveness and a Paradise as wide as the heavens and earth, extending the focus verse's reward horizon.
Wealth and children are a trial, while a great reward is with God, directly qualifying fascination with material abundance.
One who transgresses and prefers worldly life reaches the Fire, a direct warning against the valuation reversed in 28:80.
One who fears standing before the Lord and restrains desire reaches the Garden, supplying the positive alternative to worldly preference.
It diagnoses the preference for worldly life that the focus verse corrects.
The hereafter is declared better and more enduring, concisely stating the focus verse's central comparison.
Competition for accumulation distracts until the grave, exposing the danger of treating amassed wealth as lasting success.
